plus.analyst_notes:
Closes https://github.com/vz-risk/VCDB/issues/23121
Crypto-theft coding convention used throughout this batch: stolen funds coded as confidentiality data variety Virtual currency (data_victim Victim organization unless customer wallets were drained), integrity Fraudulent transaction for the unauthorized transfers, and the USD loss in impact (Asset and fraud). Tag Hacking-ext-exploit-vuln not followed: early reports guessed a minting-contract bug, but Resolv's post-mortem says the root cause was credential compromise (contractor-linked third-party project -> GitHub credentials -> malicious workflow -> cloud signing-key access policy changed). Coded hacking Use of stolen creds, vectors Partner (entry through a contractor-linked project) and Other; integrity Modify privileges (access policies changed) and Fraudulent transaction (80M USR minted and sold). Assets: S - Code repository (GitHub), S - Secrets vault (signing key; the exact cloud service is not named, closest enum), S - Other (minting contract). Cloud External Cloud Asset(s).
The contractor's third-party project was the entry point, so a provider perspective could be argued, but it is unnamed and the issue is not tagged Partner_Breach; Resolv kept as primary victim.
Data: about $25M extracted -> Virtual currency; credentials -> Credentials. Discovery: Resolv says its monitoring flagged the activity -> internal Infrastructure monitoring.
Victim country/headcount Unknown. dbir_year 2027. Main detail source is a KuCoin news flash summarizing the post-mortem; the post-mortem itself was not read.

event_chain.summary: Contractor-linked GitHub credentials used to reach repos
80M USR minted and swapped for ~$25M ETH

summary: On March 22, 2026 an attacker minted 80 million unbacked USR stablecoins from the Resolv protocol after depositing about 200,000 USDC, then swapped them for about $25 million in ETH, breaking USR's peg. Resolv's post-mortem says attackers first compromised a third-party project tied to a contractor account, exposing GitHub credentials; they used these to reach internal repositories, deployed a malicious workflow to collect more credentials, mapped the cloud infrastructure and changed access policies tied to a signing key used for minting.
